item.title: What Are the Characteristics of True Heroes?
item.description:
Cross-Cultural Psychology

What Are the Characteristics of True Heroes?

One's answer depends, in part, on their cultural background and values.

Posted September 18, 2026

Rank these six individuals according to how well they fit your definition of a true hero.

A. Man who rushes into a burning house to rescue a small child.

B. Civil rights activist and Baptist minister Martin Luther King, Jr.

C. The American soldier who saved his platoon by single-handedly eliminating a German machine-gun nest.

D. Singer, songwriter, and philanthropist Dolly Parton.

E. The student protester in 1989 who stood resolutely in front of an advancing tank in Beijing’s Tiananmen Square.

F. Political activist and media personality Charlie Kirk.

Did you place persons A and C in the top two spots? If so, why? What makes those individuals more heroic than the others?

For decades, psychologists have sought to understand how we determine whether someone is a hero or not. Is there a (presumably rare) combination of personal traits and characteristics that unequivocally signifies heroism?

Over the years, Elaine Kinsella, a research psychologist at the University of Limerick in Ireland and a leading expert on the psychology of heroes, and her colleagues have asked thousands of adults in Europe and the United States to list the personal characteristics of a hero. The dozen or so traits mentioned most frequently include brave, morally righteous, courageous, self-sacrificing, protective of others, and inspiring (Kinsella, Ritchie, and Igou, 2016). That’s why the man who rushes into a burning house to rescue a small child is considered a hero. He checks all the right boxes.

The characteristics of heroes in these studies represent the views of individuals living in Western nations. Might the markers of heroism be different in non-Western societies?

Two years ago, Kinsella and her team asked hundreds of adults in China and the United States to identify the central, prototypical characteristics of heroes (Sun, Kinsella, and Igou, 2024). Not surprisingly, several characteristics—brave, fearless, humble, helpful, and selfless—appeared frequently on the lists generated by both cultural groups. Other traits, however, were much more likely to be listed by one group than by the other.

Specifically, Chinese respondents were more likely than Americans to say that patriotism, righteousness, and respectability are defining characteristics of heroism. In contrast, Americans were more likely than Chinese to say that strength, altruism, and honesty are the traits of heroes.

The Curious Case of Social Heroes

Kinsella’s team also observed cultural similarities and differences in the kinds of acts that count as heroic. Chinese and American participants, for example, agreed that ordinary citizens who act bravely to protect or rescue people are heroes. The Good Samaritan who jumps onto subway tracks to lift a person to safety is clearly a hero in the eyes of most people, regardless of national background.

However, a particular kind of person is seen as more heroic in China than in the United States. Kinsella and others call this kind of person a social hero.

A social hero is an individual who strives tirelessly and makes personal sacrifices to achieve a greater social good. Mohandas Gandhi, Nelson Mandela, Greta Thunberg, and Malala Yousafzai are prototypical examples of social heroes.

Social heroes need not be famous. They can be a dogged scientist, a religious martyr, a persecuted freedom fighter, a whistleblower, an explorer, or a dedicated public servant (Zimbardo, 2007).

Why are social heroes seen as more heroic in China than in the United States? And why are patriotism and respectability defining characteristics of heroism in China but not in the U.S.?

The Impact of Cultural Values

According to Kinsella and her colleagues, the answers to these questions are rooted in the different values associated with individualism and collectivism (Sun, Kinsella, and Igou, 2024). One of their studies measured levels of individualism and collectivism among hundreds of American and Chinese adults. As expected, Chinese respondents were more collectivistic, on average, and Americans were more individualistic.

Collectivists place the well-being of the group (family, nation) over the well-being of the individual. A person who sacrifices his or her own self-interest for the good of the larger group is especially valorized in collectivist cultures. Metaphorically waving the flag of your family or nation is patriotic and respectable, even heroic; waving your own flag is not.

Kinsella’s team found that collectivists, regardless of their nationality and ethnicity, were more likely than individualists to say that a person who “led a successful campaign for the country’s independence, and in turn, inspired movements for civil rights and freedom across the world” was a hero (Sun, Kinsella, and Igou, 2024). That kind of person—a dedicated activist who inspires a social movement—is a social hero, and collectivists are more likely than individualists to judge such persons as patriotic and true heroes.

That’s probably why I ranked Dolly Parton and Charlie Kirk as less heroic than the others. Parton and Kirk lived lives of purpose and inspired others, but they did not sacrifice their own safety to rescue or protect someone in danger. They were social heroes. I am an American and an individualist. A social hero is admirable, but a social hero may be less heroic than the man who rushes into a burning house to rescue a small child.

item.title: Do You See the Abuse, or Simply Repeat It?
item.description:
Emotional Abuse

Do You See the Abuse, or Simply Repeat It?

Albert Bandura believed people learn by observing the behavior of others.

Posted September 18, 2026

Key points
  • Treating people in disrespectful and controlling ways has become normalized.
  • People are more likely to copy abusive behavior that gets rewarded.
  • Silence endorses abuse; action protects those who endure it.
Source: iStock / skynesher

In the 1960s, psychologist Albert Bandura developed social learning theory. His theory explains why children (and adults who sometimes think like children) do things no one ever consciously taught them to do.

Bandura believed that people learn to behave in new ways and develop new attitudes and values not by listening to and reasoning with their teachers, parents, or role models but by observing the behavior of others.

Now, consider: We live in an abusive society, where it’s normal to treat people in disrespectful and controlling ways. Don’t believe me? Tune into the media or politics or watch a movie or TV show. For many of us, we can also take a look at our family life.

For simplicity’s sake, we’ll just be looking at one type of verbal abuse (name-calling) because it’s an objective measure that requires no bias to observe or interpret.

Observing the Abuse

Many of our fellow citizens, including millions of children, see people calling each other names on a daily basis. In some cases, the name-calling is celebrated. For example, after watching, say, a woman getting demeaned by a politician on TV, they see the delighted faces of those who support the abuser.

Bandura would point to all this and say, “Aha, vicarious reinforcement!” We are all, he believed, more likely to copy behaviors we see rewarded in such a way, and so the abusive behavior spreads.

4 Stages to Thinking Abuse Is Normal

There are four stages to our thinking abuse is normal.

  1. At whatever age, I notice the abusive behavior and become riveted to its taboo nature.
  2. The incident forms a lasting memory that later informs my mimicry of that behavior.
  3. When the moment seems right, I recreate the behavior (just like my hero!), and then I look around me, expecting the same outcome my role model experienced.
  4. The people around me laugh in gleeful satisfaction and slap my back in support. I’m rewarded by this affirmation, and now I look forward to the next time I can use this technique for more of that delicious affirmation.

Bandura also noted the need for the right mental state for all this to be learned, despite its appalling behavior. The person who’s becoming abusive has to have irrational beliefs, such as “Winning is the only important thing” or “They’re out to get us, and we have to get them before they do.”

We’re Teaching Our Children to Be Abusive

For the child watching all this in their living room at home, the lesson is obvious: There’s nothing inherently wrong with verbal abuse. This may not seem like a big deal to some people; however, as I’ve observed in working with abusive men for over 35 years, verbal abuse is the chilling foreplay that always precedes violence.

Who Do You Want to Be?

So, for Bandura, after observing the behavior of others, we get to decide what person we wish to be:

  • Are you the person who sees the bully “winning” and revels in the win?
  • Or, are you the person who sees the bully and sticks up for the ones getting bullied?

When you make your decision, remember there’s a catch: If we do not call the bully’s behavior out for what it is, we have no right to expect others to stick up for our precious loved ones or us when it’s our turn to be abused by the bully. You also get to decide what kind of society you’d like to have a hand in building: an abusive, disrespectful, and controlling society or one that is free and civil, where we can walk about feeling safe from verbal abuse.

item.title: The Illusion of the "Everywhere Millionaire"
item.description:
Decision-Making

The Illusion of the "Everywhere Millionaire"

Extreme success stories trick us into ignoring underlying probabilities.

Posted September 18, 2026

Key points
  • People often misjudge a person's job by relying on descriptive traits while ignoring base rate probabilities.
  • Success stories focusing on the "winner" miss how rare it is to get there.
  • Major life choices should not rely on outlier success stories that ignore basic odds.
Stories of an individual often neglect the underlying probabilities
Source: Generated by ChatGPT/ Concept by Arturo Hernandez

In my cognitive psychology class, there’s a section on reasoning and problem-solving where I always ask students to answer a question. It’s a demo originally used by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky.

Steve is very shy and withdrawn, invariably helpful but with very little interest in people or in the world of reality. A meek and tidy soul, he has a need for order and structure, and a passion for detail.

Is he a physician, farmer, salesperson, or librarian?

When I ask students in my class, the overwhelming majority answer "librarian." Why? Because Steve is a meek and tidy soul. He’s introverted. He has his own world. Librarians presumably like to be organized, because you have to organize the books in the stacks. They tend to be quiet and introverted because they like books. So Steve must be a librarian.

The better bet is "salesperson." Why? Because there aren’t a lot of librarian jobs. There are about 140,000 librarians in the United States and more than 13 million people working in sales. Students still say librarian. Why is that?

They pick Steve based on what he is like and ignore how many people hold each job. They’re going by the diagnostic information, the information about the individual, and not the probability that someone holds that job.

The Temptation of Outlier Narratives

Recently, Apple News has been playing a similar trick, though not exactly the same—it keeps feeding me this story in The Wall Street Journal about Everywhere Millionaires.

It’s adapted from a book by two economists. They even have a picture of Dick Portillo. He started a hot dog business, sold it for a billion dollars, and now owns a yacht. They call them Everywhere Millionaires because they’re in every town, running ordinary businesses like HVAC contractors, vet practices, and local restaurant chains. But they’re everyday people. They didn’t do some kind of self-driving car or a rocket ship or new software that everybody owns. In the case of Dick Portillo, he just started a hot dog business.

The message is a nice one. You don’t have to do something incredibly fancy to live a life of wealth. You can start a small business and, over time, be very wealthy and live extremely well. But here’s the catch.

Steve and Dick are the same faulty reasoning running in opposite directions. In the case of Steve, people think he should be a librarian because he fits the description. They forget to think about how many people have the job. In the case of Dick, people look at the result—his wealth. What they don’t think about is how likely it is that someone who opens a hot dog stand eventually sells it for a billion dollars. They are both neglecting the underlying probability of an event. And in both cases, the probabilities are very low.

Uncovering Survivor Bias

I kept reading and reading, because it reminded me of an article I wrote, “The Sample Is Already Sorted.” So I kept reading until they finally told me how many of these Everywhere Millionaires there are. Three million, in a country of about 340 million people. Depending on whether you count people or households, that’s somewhere between 1 in 100 and 1 in 50. That means out of every hundred people you see, one or two of them will be like this.

So some of those three million might be sitting a few rows behind you at your son’s game. At a ballpark with 40,000 people, that’s a few hundred of them. The authors say one of them might be coaching your kid’s soccer team. That’s probably true. Dick Portillo won’t be. He’s on a 130-foot yacht called Top Dog, docked behind his house in Naples, Florida. He’s not a typical Everywhere Millionaire. He’s the far end of the tail, and that’s the one they put in the picture.

Opening a business is easy. You can file the paperwork to get an LLC, or whatever mechanism you want to use, and with that, you can open a business. But then that business has to survive, and roughly a third of businesses survive 10 years. Dick Portillo’s business survived 50 years.

When we start with a successful millionaire like Portillo and go back in time, it becomes easy to trace what steps led to what result. But the question is, how many people also went down the same path and were not successful? How many decided to take other jobs, drive an Uber, or work at a coffee shop? The answer is, we don’t know.

Evaluating Base Rates

To be fair, the authors are economists, and they know about base rates. They point out that most successful founders come from poor or middle-class families, simply because there are so many more people in the bottom 99 percent than in the top one percent. That’s the Steve problem, solved correctly. But notice in which direction they follow it. They start with the founders and ask where they came from. In this essay, they never start with everyone who tried and ask how many made it. They tell us a rich kid has six times the chance of starting a successful business as a poor kid. Six times what? They don’t say.

So we can go back to Steve and my classroom example. Let’s imagine that Steve really is a librarian. If you only looked at librarians, you’d find plenty of meek and tidy souls who love books and have a strong inner world, and you’d conclude that’s the path to being a librarian. The thought experiment turns it around for us. Most meek and tidy souls aren’t librarians. And most people who open a hot dog stand never sell it for a billion dollars. The essay ends by saying someone has to build these businesses, and “it might as well be you.” Maybe. If you love hot dogs, or just had the wild idea of opening one, by all means follow your instinct. But don’t expect the yacht. In other words, don’t take life-changing advice based on a story in The Wall Street Journal.

item.title: The Beauty of Space
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

The Beauty of Space

Japanese aesthetics show how to protect our cognitive integrity during AI use.

Posted September 18, 2026

Key points
  • Japanese aesthetics treats space, or ma, not as absence but as an active form worth protecting.
  • Constant engagement and oversight of AI systems can be balanced with intentional reflection and space.
  • Pausing is not inefficiency; it keeps judgment, agency, and sense of self—our cognitive integrity—intact.
Source: Marlynn Wei / Met Museum, Rei Kawakubo, Art of the In-between, 2017

MA
The garden is a medium
for meditation
Perceive the blankness
Listen to the voice of the
silence
Imagine the void filled

— Arata Isozaki, Japanese architect

“Too much furniture in a home; too many Buddha figures in a temple; too many stones and plants in the garden.”

— Kenkō, Japanese monk, Tsurezuregusa, 1330-1332

In 2017, I walked slowly in between the black and red shapes and forms against the bright white empty space created in the Met Museum exhibition by Comme des Garçons founder and Tokyo-based designer Rei Kawakubo’s Art of the In-between. I have kept my copy of the slim, black-and-white exhibition guide for all these years. Kawakubo’s creations are closely related to the Japanese concepts of ma (space) and mu (emptiness), which “coexist in the concept of the in-between.”

The Japanese character for ma (間), for space, gap, interval, or pause, combines the character for “gate” (門) with “sun” below (日), creating the shape of light coming through a doorway. In this image, the space becomes the object.

This memory came to me from creating space to engage with the first exercise of a prompt writing book (three six five by Lucy Ives). Day one: “Walk to a place where you can sit awhile undisturbed. Now write a detailed account of how you got there. The shorter the trip, the longer the account should be.”

I took five steps, coffee in hand, from the couch to a writing desk and started to write.

And this—the memory of “ma” and the quiet steps inside the Met Museum exhibit—is where I ended up. When we give our mind space as an active place, described by John Stevens as an “active absence,” something unexpected may come to exist.

Intentional Space

As Japanese avant-garde filmmaker and artist Takahiko Iimura explains, “Negative space does not necessarily mean non-existence but has a form of existence.”

Source: Takahiko Iimura, Between the Frames MA series (1-13), photographic prints on mount board, 2010

But with the rush to be more efficient and produce more, faster, how often are we giving ourselves this space these days?

In Japanese architecture, the tokonoma is an alcove space which is created intentionally for flowers or a sculpture. In the floral-arranging practice of ikebana, there is also value in creating space in between the stems and blossoms—it is not about filling the vase to the fullest. In a practice found in the Zen ink paintings of the feudal period, yohaku-no-bi (the beauty of blank space), the painting composition is intentionally left with space.

As Mitsuo Inoue describes in Space in Japanese Architecture, during the Japanese medieval period, the Buddhist ideas of “emptiness” and “nothingness” became prominent.

Nowadays, voids are hard to come by.

The Concept of Ma and AI Use

This is not a case against AI, but one that supports a collaborative approach and considers our ability to create space around our interactions with AI systems. The risk of overseeing and engaging with the ceaseless generation of AI system outputs, including large language models and AI agents, includes cognitive strain, attention depletion, information overload, and decision fatigue (“AI brain fry”).

Pause, too, can be a form of work.

The concept of ma has a different resonance than applying cognitive friction, a proposed method to counter the negative cognitive effects of overreliance on AI. The study found that cognitive friction was effective in reducing overreliance on AI systems—participants accepted fewer wrong AI answers when forced to engage first. But cognitive friction design came with a major tradeoff: people enjoyed it less. The people who benefited the most from cognitive friction interventions were those who are most inclined to think things through analytically and also were most annoyed by it. Seeing ma as an intentional space that we can create—to slow down in increments—keeps our human judgment, agency, empathy, and sense of self at the center.

Treating empty space, a pause, an interval as an aesthetic form in itself is different than seeing it as an intrusion or break. This space, our cognitive space and capacity for reflection, is worth protecting; it protects us in return.

Marlynn Wei, M.D., PLLC Copyright 2026. All Rights Reserved.
